questions.prompt: What is the root cause of injection vulnerabilities?

options.text: Untrusted input is mixed into a command so it can change the command's structure
Passwords stored with a slow hash

questions.explanation: Injection happens when untrusted input is interpreted as part of a command/query; the interpreter can't separate intended code from injected input.

questions.prompt: What is the primary, reliable fix for SQL injection?
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries fix the query structure and bind user values as pure data, so input can never change the query — the reliable cure for SQLi.

questions.prompt: For input validation, prefer an ____-list of known-good values over a deny-list.
questions.explanation: Allow-lists permit only known-good values; deny-lists try to block known-bad and are routinely bypassed with encodings and edge cases.

questions.prompt: Which measures help defend against injection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Calling programs with an argument list instead of a shell string
Concatenating user input directly into SQL

questions.explanation: Parameterized queries, argument-list APIs, and least-privilege accounts defend against injection; string concatenation is the vulnerability itself.

questions.prompt: Match each injection type to what it targets.
questions.explanation: Each injection targets a different interpreter, but all share the same cause and fix: keep code and data separate via safe APIs.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to properly fix a concatenated SQL query.

items.text: Parameterize the query (bind values as data)
Add input validation as defense in depth
Run under a least-privilege DB account
Verify the injection input no longer works

questions.explanation: Parameterization is the essential fix; validation and least privilege add depth; then verify the payload is neutralized.
